cues: What holds in the storm? Picture the Sahara, the largest hot desert on earth, about the size of the United States. There are sand seas so wide you can walk for days and see nothing but dunes.

For centuries, Timbuktu sat at its southern edge, a city of scholars and traders, and twice a year a great caravan called the azalai sets out north from Timbuktu to a place called Taoudenni, where men cut slabs of salt out of the earth. It's about 430 miles.
Three weeks walking there, three weeks back. In the old days, several thousand camels walked in one line, each carrying four or five slabs of salt, or about 66 pounds each.
The one who leads it is the khabir, the guide. There's no road and no compass, so how does he find the way? By day he reads the sand. The wind builds the dunes the same way across the whole desert.
A gentle slope on one side, a steep face on the other. A good guide can feel that slope under his feet and hold his direction, even in the dark. By night he read the stars.
The sand and the stars fail at different times, so together they never fail at once.
But the hardest job isn't direction, it's water. For six weeks he has to know how many days since the last well and how many to the next.
One mistake and the whole caravan dies of thirst.
So he doesn't keep a number in his head. He keeps the places, every well, and every landmark, named in order.
Then the sandstorms come. The sky turns orange, then brown.
And a wall of sand rolls in. It is not like weather. It is like a door closing.
And here is what the khabir does. He stops.
The men put the camels down.
Sit among them, cover their faces, and wait.
His job in a storm is not to make progress.
It is not to get lost and to pick up the way again when the air clears.
Because the ridges are still there.
None of this was written in a book.
It passed from uncle to nephew and father to son on foot.
The azalai still walks today, even as the trucks take its place.
We all go through storms at work and at home.
In a storm you lose your sleep, your judgment, and your sense of time.
But some things are still true.
This week, name the storm you're in.
Or the last one you came through.
Write down what stayed true through it.
Pick the plainest one and put it on a card you keep with you.
When the next storm hits, stop.
Sit down, breathe in for four, out for six, and wait for the air to clear.
The ridges will still be there.
Thank you.
